records.name: Bolívar
records.current_summary:
The murder of Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader who campaigned with the "No Es Hora De Callar" movement and joined its sixth symbolic return march of 500+ survivors of sexual violence, is documented in Bolívar on 22 May 2025; she was killed in Carmen de Bolívar, and more than 19 days after the killing the circumstances of what happened remain unclear (friend and fellow leader Yirley Velasco recalls her as a trans-rights fighter in the municipality). El Tiempo's data-journalism work on the gap between official Fiscalía and NGO (Caribe Afirmativo/Defensoría) figures names her case specifically. Bolívar appears within the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged by Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 territorial-expansion finding, where state response is weakest.

Versus the national score (~0.52), Bolívar sits approximately 0.08 lower: the killing is a named, targeted murder of a community leader (not an undifferentiated count), and the department falls within the "territorial expansion" zone where the monitoring body documents insufficient state protection. Versus Antioquia (0.33), Bolívar is substantially higher because it carries one specific high-profile homicide rather than the 45-of-270 structural concentration and multi-case impunity pattern defining Antioquia. Versus Atlántico (0.43), Bolívar is marginally above: its evidence is a single named killing within an aggregate warning, whereas Atlántico carries a forward-looking escalation call-out tied to a larger trans sex-work hub.
records.current_localsOnly: The victim's community-leadership world - the symbolic return march of 500+ sexual-violence survivors she took part in - is resident- and survivor-facing; the visitor-facing signal is the named targeted killing of an activist inside an expansion zone where state protection is documented as weakest.

sources.claim: El Tiempo data investigation (2025): Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader who had campaigned with the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement and joined its sixth symbolic return march of more than 500 survivors of sexual violence, was killed - the article calls it a trans feminicide - in Bolívar on 22 May, in Carmen de Bolívar; more than 19 days later the circumstances remained unclear, and friend and fellow social leader Yirley Velasco remembers her as having taken up the fight for trans rights in the municipality. The piece exposes the gap between official and NGO figures: the Fiscalía's own data base records 3,322 intentional homicides of people identified as LGBTIQ+ between January 2010 and May 2025, 431 for 2024 versus about 160 reported by the NGO (267 fewer), and 39 homicides in one Fiscalía dependency's 2025 data versus 156 in the policies-and-strategies base; experts cited describe the information system as neither unified nor reliable.

Caribe Afirmativo's own 2025 report 'Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia': in 2025 one LGBTIQ+ person was killed every 32 hours, violence escalates along a continuum (discrimination to intrafamily violence, 1,531 cases; sexual violence, 628 cases; threats, 1,184 victims; homicide; impunity) and the report documents territorial expansion of the violence towards territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, alongside insufficient state response. The cached text does not name Bolívar explicitly; it supports the record's claim that Bolívar sits within the Caribbean-coast cluster flagged for territorial expansion where state response is weakest, the named killing itself being covered by the El Tiempo verdict.

records.name: Caldas
records.current_summary:
No Caldas-specific law, enforcement practice or incident finding for trans people appears in the record's surviving sources. The national reporting they carry frames what a visitor stands under anywhere in the country: an English-language international paper (April 2025) reported the killing of Sara Millerey, a trans woman beaten in daylight and filmed by onlookers in a northern metropolitan area, whose death from her injuries provoked national alarm over transfemicide; and an international daily's investigation (July 2024) documented armed groups in a southern department circulating 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women and forcing them from their homes, with dozens killed nationally.

Those reported cases concern other departments. Nothing here marks Caldas as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture, and because such violence surfaces where monitors and journalists can reach, the absence of Caldas-specific findings is weak evidence of safety, not proof of it.

sources.claim: El País English edition (14 April 2025) reports Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman beaten in broad daylight in Bello, Antioquia, filmed by onlookers and thrown into a creek, who died of a second cardiac arrest the following afternoon with no one arrested; the article states hate crimes killed 13 trans people in Colombia in the first quarter of 2025 and that her death provoked national outrage and mobilisations against transphobia. That national transfemicide alarm is the picture this department is assessed against; the report contains no Caldas-specific information.

The Guardian investigation (30 July 2024) documents armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women, quotes an activist saying the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide (recording the killings as ordinary cases), and reports 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024. This national armed-group violence and displacement baseline is what this department is assessed against; the report contains no Caldas-specific information.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Colombia - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's Colombia country overview confirms the dated national baseline a visitor to Meta stands under: consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981; the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, making Colombia the fourth Latin American country to do so, and same-sex couples have had full adoption rights since 2015; a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; the right to change legal gender is recognised since 1993 and without psychiatric or physical evaluations; a national LGBTI policy text addresses rights in public education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict and says national entities may not refuse to recognise them. The page carries no Meta-specific content, so it supplies only the framework against which the record's 'no Meta-specific finding' assessment and its armed-conflict displacement dynamic sit.

records.name: Cundinamarca
records.current_summary:

A second cited item documents the widely shared killing of a trans woman in a northern city that prompted national alarm (April 2025) — reported in Antioquia, not here.

Nothing in the record marks Cundinamarca as materially safer or more dangerous than that national picture, and the absence of Cundinamarca-specific findings reflects where such violence gets reported, not proven safety.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Colombia - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's 'LGBTQ rights in Colombia' page states the national framework a visitor stands under in Cundinamarca: since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on their Colombian birth certificate, with current options F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero). On 9 July 2026 outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo signed Decree 0732 of 2026, which obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request (and a simultaneous name change) free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure. The Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 ruling ordered the government to offer the nonbinary ('NB') option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws, and since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options (male, female, X). A 2016 report (Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS) documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity. Gender-marker change is a notarial/bureaucratic process with no surgery or court ruling required and applies equally in Cundinamarca.

sources.title: LGBT rights in Colombia - Wikipedia
sources.claim: National-framework article governing what a visitor stands under in Magdalena, whose own dossier records no department-specific trans finding. It records that consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981; Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011; the right to change legal gender has existed since 1993, and since 2015 gender change is possible without psychiatric or physical evaluations. The Constitutional Court legalized same-sex marriage in April 2016 (fourth Latin American country) and granted same-sex couples full adoption rights in 2015; transgender people have been allowed to serve openly in the military since 2015. It also reports Colombian society as 'generally conservative' on LGBT issues, with an October 2019 Invamer poll reaching 50% support for same-sex marriage for the first time (47% opposed). The article carries no Magdalena-specific fact, so like the record's existing CNN and Guardian sources it grounds the national framework a visitor in this department stands under rather than a department-level finding.
